concept.name: Large-lot trade
concept.definition: A single executed trade (or an exchange-fragmented series of prints from one large order) whose size is far above the typical trade size for that instrument, taken in order-flow practice as a sign of institutional participation. Platforms surface them with filters that flag prints above absolute or adaptive size thresholds.
concept.intuition: Retail trades in ones and tens; when a 2,000-lot print hits the tape, someone with serious size is doing business.
concept.mechanics: Detected by scanning the time-and-sales stream for trades exceeding a fixed or adaptive threshold (platforms such as ATAS re-aggregate the fragmented prints exchange matching algorithms produce and mark the consolidated size on the chart).
concept.failure_modes: Large prints include spread rolls, block reporting, and opening/closing auction volume, which carry different information than directional institutional aggression; size thresholds that work in one volatility regime mislead in another.
concept.misconceptions: A large print is not automatically 'smart money' to follow — the initiator may be liquidating, hedging, or rolling, and the print says nothing about their remaining intent.
concept.example: On a day when the median ES trade is 3 contracts, the tape prints a single 1,800-lot at the offer near a session high; the platform flags it and the trader watches whether price accepts above that level.

citations.source: ATAS — Trading Indicators (Big Trades: high-volume market trades, aggregated vs fragmented prints)
